questions.stem: A mobile app lets users sign in with their Google accounts. After sign-in, the app must upload files directly to Amazon S3 with temporary AWS credentials. Which steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Sign users in with an Amazon Cognito user pool federated with Google
options.rationale: The user pool handles sign-in, including federation with social identity providers.

options.text: Create an IAM user for each app user
options.rationale: IAM users are for long-term identities, not for large numbers of app users.

options.text: Give each user an API Gateway API key
options.rationale: API keys identify clients for usage plans; they do not grant AWS credentials.

options.text: Use an Amazon Cognito identity pool to get temporary AWS credentials
options.rationale: Identity pools exchange the user's token for temporary credentials for an IAM role.

options.text: Embed one IAM access key in the mobile app and share it across all users
options.rationale: Keys in an app can be extracted and are shared by everyone.

questions.explanation: User pools authenticate users; identity pools turn that sign-in into temporary AWS credentials.

questions.stem: A REST API in Amazon API Gateway must accept only requests from users who signed in through an Amazon Cognito user pool. What should the developer configure?

options.text: IAM authorization on each method, with clients sending their user pool user name and password
options.rationale: IAM authorization expects SigV4-signed requests, not passwords.

options.text: A Cognito user pool authorizer, with clients sending their token in the Authorization header
options.rationale: API Gateway validates the token against the user pool before calling the backend.

options.text: An API key required on each method
options.rationale: API keys are not a way to authenticate individual users.

options.text: A CORS configuration that allows the user pool's domain
options.rationale: CORS controls browser origins, not user authentication.

questions.explanation: Cognito user pool authorizers let API Gateway verify user pool tokens without custom code.

questions.stem: Users must be able to download private reports from an Amazon S3 bucket for 15 minutes after they request them. The bucket must stay private. What should the application do?

options.text: Make each report public, then delete it with a scheduled job after 15 minutes
options.rationale: Public objects are open to anyone who finds the URL.

options.text: Add a bucket policy that allows anonymous reads
options.rationale: This makes every object in the bucket public.

options.text: Generate a presigned URL for the object with a 15-minute expiry
options.rationale: A presigned URL grants time-limited access with the signer's permissions.

options.text: Give each user IAM access keys for the bucket
options.rationale: Distributing long-term keys is risky and hard to revoke.

questions.explanation: Presigned URLs give temporary access to a private object without changing the bucket's permissions.

questions.stem: A web application lets users upload files directly from the browser to a private Amazon S3 bucket, without sending the files through the application's servers. What should the backend give the browser?

options.text: The backend's IAM access keys, sent over HTTPS for safety
options.rationale: Exposing keys in the browser gives anyone full use of them.

options.text: A public bucket name with write access for everyone
options.rationale: Anyone could upload anything to the bucket.

options.text: A CloudFront signed cookie
options.rationale: Signed cookies control access to content served through CloudFront, not direct uploads to S3.

options.text: A presigned URL for a PUT request to the object's key
options.rationale: The browser uploads straight to S3 with the URL, which expires after a set time.

questions.explanation: Presigned URLs work for uploads as well as downloads.

questions.stem: A video site serves premium content through Amazon CloudFront. Subscribers must be able to watch many video segment files without the site changing every file URL. What should the developer use?

options.text: CloudFront signed cookies
options.rationale: Signed cookies grant access to many files without changing their URLs.

options.text: CloudFront signed URLs for each segment file
options.rationale: Signed URLs work per file, so every segment URL would change.

options.text: S3 presigned URLs to the origin bucket
options.rationale: Presigned URLs bypass CloudFront and still change each URL.

options.text: A public origin bucket with obscure file names
options.rationale: Hidden names are not access control.

questions.explanation: Use signed URLs for individual files and signed cookies for many files or when URLs must stay the same.

questions.stem: An application that runs under an IAM role in account A must read items from a DynamoDB table in account B by using temporary credentials. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Allow the application's role in account A to call sts:AssumeRole on that role
options.rationale: Account A must also permit its principal to assume the role; AWS STS then returns temporary credentials.

options.text: Create an IAM user in account B and store that user's access keys in the application
options.rationale: Access keys are long-term credentials, which the requirement rules out, and they are harder to secure and rotate.

options.text: Copy the table to account A every hour
options.rationale: Copying data adds cost and staleness instead of granting access.

options.text: Peer the VPCs in the two accounts so the application can reach the table
options.rationale: DynamoDB access is controlled by IAM; network connectivity does not grant permissions.

options.text: In account B, create a role that trusts account A and allows reads on the table
options.rationale: The role's trust policy names account A, and its permissions policy grants read access to the table.

questions.explanation: Cross-account role access needs a role in account B that trusts account A, plus permission in account A to assume it; STS then issues temporary credentials. An IAM user in account B is the nearest distractor, but its keys are long-term credentials.

questions.stem: An application on Amazon EC2 instances must write to an Amazon S3 bucket. How should the application get AWS credentials?

options.text: Store an IAM user's access keys in the credentials file on each instance
options.rationale: Long-term keys on disk can leak and must be rotated by hand.

options.text: Put the root user's access keys in environment variables
options.rationale: Root keys should never be used by applications.

options.text: Attach an IAM role through an instance profile and let the SDK find it
options.rationale: The SDK's default credential chain finds the role's temporary credentials automatically.

options.text: Hardcode access keys in the application source
options.rationale: Keys in code end up in repositories and builds.

questions.explanation: Roles give applications temporary credentials that rotate automatically.

questions.stem: Developers need to run AWS CLI commands from their laptops. They sign in to AWS through the company's AWS access portal in IAM Identity Center, and the company does not want long-term access keys on laptops. What should the developers do?

options.text: Create IAM access keys for each developer and rotate them every month with a script
options.rationale: This still leaves long-term keys on laptops.

options.text: Share one administrator's access keys
options.rationale: Shared keys remove accountability and give everyone the same broad access.

options.text: Use the console password as the CLI secret key
options.rationale: Console passwords cannot sign API requests.

options.text: Use an IAM Identity Center profile in the CLI and run aws sso login
options.rationale: The CLI retrieves temporary credentials for the profile's role and renews them while the IAM Identity Center session is valid.

questions.explanation: IAM Identity Center profiles, set up with aws configure sso, give the CLI temporary credentials without stored keys.

questions.stem: A company requires MFA before a developer can call the API that deletes production data. The developer uses the AWS CLI with an IAM user. Which steps will enforce this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add an MFA condition to the KMS key policy
options.rationale: The requirement is on the delete API, not on a KMS key.

options.text: Add an aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition to the delete permission
options.rationale: The action is allowed only when the request's credentials came from an MFA sign-in.

options.text: Enable MFA on the account's root user
options.rationale: Root MFA protects the root user, not this developer's API calls.

options.text: Call sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity and pass the developer's IAM password
options.rationale: That API exchanges web identity tokens, not passwords.

options.text: Call sts:GetSessionToken with an MFA code and use those credentials
options.rationale: Temporary credentials obtained with MFA carry the MFA context.

questions.explanation: MFA-protected API access combines a policy condition with temporary credentials obtained using MFA.

questions.stem: A Lambda function must be invoked when objects are created in an Amazon S3 bucket. The S3 event notification fails to save because S3 is not allowed to invoke the function. What should the developer add?

options.text: Allow Amazon S3 to invoke the function in the function's resource-based policy
options.rationale: Resource-based policies grant other services permission to invoke a function.

options.text: Add Amazon S3 read and write permissions for the bucket to the function's execution role
options.rationale: The execution role controls what the function can call, not who can call it.

options.text: Add a bucket policy that allows the function to read objects
options.rationale: Reading objects is separate from S3 invoking the function.

options.text: Create an IAM user for Amazon S3 to use
options.rationale: Services are granted access through policies, not IAM users.

questions.explanation: Execution role: what the function may do. Resource-based policy: who may invoke the function.

questions.stem: A backend service calls a REST API in Amazon API Gateway that uses IAM authorization. The service sends plain HTTP requests without an AWS SDK, and every call is rejected. What must the service do?

options.text: Add an x-api-key header with a valid API key to each request
options.rationale: API keys do not satisfy IAM authorization.

options.text: Sign each request with Signature Version 4 (SigV4)
options.rationale: IAM-authorized APIs accept requests signed with SigV4 (or SigV4a) by principals with execute-api:Invoke permission.

options.text: Send its IAM user name in a custom header
options.rationale: A name is not a signature and proves nothing.

options.text: Call the API over HTTP instead of HTTPS
options.rationale: Dropping TLS weakens security and does not authenticate the request.

questions.explanation: SDKs and the CLI sign requests automatically; raw HTTP clients must add SigV4 signing.

questions.stem: A REST API in Amazon API Gateway must authorize each request by checking a custom API token in a request header against the company's own token database. What should the developer configure?

options.text: An Amazon Cognito user pool authorizer for the API's methods
options.rationale: A Cognito authorizer validates tokens issued by a Cognito user pool, not tokens from the company's own database.

options.text: A Lambda authorizer that validates the token and returns an IAM policy
options.rationale: A Lambda authorizer runs custom code to check the caller and returns a policy that allows or denies the request.

options.text: IAM authorization on the methods, with the custom token passed in the header
options.rationale: IAM authorization expects SigV4-signed requests made with AWS credentials, not a custom token.

options.text: A usage plan with API keys created from the token database
options.rationale: API keys identify callers for throttling and quotas; they are not meant for authorization.

questions.explanation: Custom authorization logic in API Gateway belongs in a Lambda authorizer.

questions.stem: A backend service with no user present must call an API that is protected by an Amazon Cognito user pool. The API checks for an OAuth scope named orders.read. How should the service get a token?

options.text: Create a Cognito user for the service and store its password in the code
options.rationale: A shared user account with a stored password is not the machine-to-machine pattern and adds a secret to the code.

options.text: Use an identity pool to get temporary AWS credentials for the service
options.rationale: Identity pool credentials sign AWS requests; they are not OAuth tokens with scopes.

options.text: Use an app client's client credentials grant and request the orders.read scope
options.rationale: The client credentials grant is the OAuth flow for machine-to-machine access, and scopes come from a resource server.

options.text: Use the authorization code grant with a redirect to the hosted sign-in page
options.rationale: The authorization code grant needs a person to sign in.

questions.explanation: For service-to-service calls, use the client credentials grant with custom scopes defined on a resource server.

questions.stem: A Lambda function's execution role allows s3:* on all resources. A bucket policy on one bucket explicitly denies s3:DeleteObject for that role. What happens when the function tries to delete an object in that bucket?

options.text: The request is allowed, because the role's identity policy is evaluated first
options.rationale: Policies are not evaluated in an order where the first match wins; an explicit deny overrides allows.

options.text: The request is allowed, because s3:* also includes the s3:DeleteObject action
options.rationale: The allow does match, but the explicit deny in the bucket policy still overrides it.

options.text: The request fails with a throttling error because the two policies conflict
options.rationale: Conflicting policies do not cause throttling; the deny simply takes effect.

options.text: The request is denied, because an explicit deny in any policy overrides every allow
options.rationale: IAM evaluates all applicable policies, and an explicit deny always wins.

questions.explanation: In IAM policy evaluation, an explicit deny in any applicable policy overrides every allow.

questions.stem: A Lambda function needs to read items from one DynamoDB table named Orders with GetItem and Query. Which execution role policy follows least privilege?

options.text: Allow dynamodb:GetItem and dynamodb:Query on the Orders table's ARN
options.rationale: This grants only the actions the function uses, on the one table it uses.

options.text: Attach the AmazonDynamoDBFullAccess managed policy to the role
options.rationale: Full access grants writes, deletes and table management on every table.

options.text: Allow dynamodb:* on the Orders table's ARN and every index ARN
options.rationale: This includes write and delete actions that the function does not need.

options.text: Allow dynamodb:GetItem and dynamodb:Query on every table in the account (*)
options.rationale: The actions are right, but every table in the account becomes readable.

questions.explanation: Least privilege means the specific actions on the specific resources the code uses.

questions.stem: A mobile app gets AWS credentials from an Amazon Cognito identity pool and calls DynamoDB directly. Each user must be able to read and write only the items whose partition key is that user's identity ID. How should the developer enforce this?

options.text: Filter the items by user ID in the app before showing them to the user
options.rationale: Client-side filtering does not stop a user from calling DynamoDB for other users' items.

options.text: A dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition set to the user's Cognito identity ID
options.rationale: The condition limits access to items whose partition key equals the caller's identity ID.

options.text: Create a separate DynamoDB table for each user of the mobile app
options.rationale: This does not scale and still needs a policy to keep users out of other tables.

options.text: Give the identity pool's authenticated role read access to the table and nothing else
options.rationale: Read-only access does not separate users' items and blocks the writes.

questions.explanation: Fine-grained access control for DynamoDB uses IAM conditions such as dynamodb:LeadingKeys with a policy variable.

questions.stem: An application in an Amazon ECS task must upload files to an Amazon S3 bucket. How should the application get AWS permissions?

options.text: Grant the permissions to the task execution role in the task definition
options.rationale: The task execution role is used by the ECS agent to pull images and send logs, not by the application.

options.text: Store an IAM user's access keys as environment variables in the task
options.rationale: Long-term keys in environment variables can leak and need manual rotation.

options.text: Grant the permissions to the task role that the task definition specifies
options.rationale: The task role provides credentials to the application code running in the task's containers.

options.text: Add the permissions to the bucket's ACL for the ECS service principal
options.rationale: ACLs and the service principal do not give a particular task's application its own permissions.

questions.explanation: Application permissions go on the task role; the execution role is for ECS itself.

questions.stem: A developer signs in to the AWS CLI with an IAM user and must run commands as the DeployRole role in the same account. Which combination of steps will let the developer do this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run aws configure with the role's ARN as the access key ID
options.rationale: A role ARN is not an access key.

options.text: Make sure DeployRole's trust policy allows the developer's IAM user to assume it
options.rationale: AssumeRole succeeds only if the role trusts the caller and the caller is allowed sts:AssumeRole.

options.text: Attach DeployRole to the IAM user as a permissions boundary
options.rationale: A permissions boundary limits the user's own permissions; it does not let the user act as the role.

options.text: Add a CLI profile with role_arn set to DeployRole and source_profile set to the user's profile
options.rationale: The CLI calls AssumeRole with the source profile's credentials and uses the temporary credentials it returns.

options.text: Create access keys for DeployRole and put them in the credentials file
options.rationale: Roles do not have long-term access keys.

questions.explanation: A CLI role profile plus a trust policy that allows the caller lets the CLI assume the role automatically.

questions.stem: A Lambda function generates presigned URLs for Amazon S3 downloads with a requested expiration of 12 hours. Users report that the links stop working after about an hour. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The bucket's lifecycle rules remove the objects after an hour
options.rationale: The scenario does not mention lifecycle rules, and the objects would be missing for every request.

options.text: Presigned URLs cannot be valid for longer than one hour
options.rationale: Presigned URLs can be valid for longer; the limit here comes from the signing credentials.

options.text: The function's timeout ends the URL's validity when it returns
options.rationale: The URL does not depend on the function staying running.

options.text: The function's temporary signing credentials expire first
options.rationale: A presigned URL stops working when the credentials that signed it expire, even if the requested expiration is later.

questions.explanation: A presigned URL is valid until its expiration time or until the signing credentials expire, whichever comes first.

questions.stem: Users of a web app sign in through an Amazon Cognito user pool, and an identity pool gives them AWS credentials. Members of the admins group need extra permissions that regular users must not get. What should the developer configure?

options.text: Identity pool role-based access that maps the admins group to its own role
options.rationale: The identity pool can choose a role from the user's groups in the user pool token, so admins get their own role.

options.text: One authenticated role for everyone, with admin checks done in the browser code
options.rationale: Checks in browser code can be bypassed, and every user still gets the same AWS permissions.

options.text: Separate user pools for admins and for regular users of the app
options.rationale: This duplicates user management and is not needed to give admins a different role.

options.text: A resource policy on each AWS resource listing the admins' user names
options.rationale: AWS resource policies do not evaluate Cognito user names.

questions.explanation: Identity pools support role-based access control, choosing an IAM role from user pool groups or rules.

questions.stem: A REST API in Amazon API Gateway in account A must be callable by an application that runs under an IAM role in account B, and by no other accounts. Which combination of steps will meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Make the API private and create a VPC endpoint in account A
options.rationale: A private API restricts network access through VPC endpoints; it does not grant account B's role access.

options.text: Add a resource policy to the API that allows execute-api:Invoke for the role in account B
options.rationale: For cross-account calls, the API's resource policy must grant access to the other account's principal.

options.text: Turn on CORS for the API's resources and methods
options.rationale: CORS controls browser cross-origin requests, not which AWS accounts can call the API.

options.text: Use IAM authorization on the methods, and sign requests with SigV4 from account B
options.rationale: IAM authorization identifies the caller from signed requests made with account B's credentials.

options.text: Create an API key in account A and share it with account B
options.rationale: API keys are for usage plans, not for authorizing an account's callers.

questions.explanation: Cross-account access to an API uses IAM authorization together with a resource policy that names the other account's principal.

questions.stem: An application signs users in with an Amazon Cognito user pool. A new requirement says users must enter a code from an authenticator app in addition to their password. What should the developer turn on?

options.text: An IAM policy condition that requires aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent
options.rationale: That condition applies to AWS API calls with IAM credentials, not to app sign-in.

options.text: MFA in the user pool, with authenticator app (TOTP) codes
options.rationale: User pools support MFA with time-based one-time passwords from authenticator apps.

options.text: A longer minimum password length in the user pool
options.rationale: A stronger password is still a single factor.

options.text: A Lambda authorizer that asks users for a second password
options.rationale: A second password is not a second factor, and authorizers do not run sign-in.

questions.explanation: Cognito user pools provide MFA for application users, including TOTP authenticator apps.

questions.stem: A CI/CD system that runs outside AWS deploys to an AWS account by using a long-term IAM access key. The security team wants to remove that key. The CI system can issue OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens. What should the developer set up?

options.text: A new access key for the IAM user every week
options.rationale: Rotating the key still leaves a long-term key in the CI system.

options.text: An Amazon Cognito user pool account for the CI system
options.rationale: A user pool signs in application users; it is not how a CI system federates to an IAM role.

options.text: An IAM OIDC provider and a role that trusts it
options.rationale: The role trusts the provider, and the CI system exchanges its token for temporary credentials (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity).

options.text: An EC2 instance profile attached to the CI system
options.rationale: Instance profiles apply to EC2 instances, not to systems outside AWS.

questions.explanation: OIDC federation gives external workloads temporary credentials without long-term keys.
